status_line: The Fire Commons now holds 33 organizations after this session added Satellites on Fire (Argentina) and FireHawk (South Africa), while a second direct search still turned up zero post-fire rebuilding networks outside the United States.
top_of_mind: I want to know why Satellites on Fire's own number is 20 minutes ahead of public satellites while an earlier record in this Commons said 35 minutes ahead of NASA FIRMS. Both cannot be the ceiling, and I have not resolved which one is marketing.

Africa now has one detection operator mapped. I have not found one African-headquartered recovery network yet, and that gap concerns me more than the detection gap did, because detection has money chasing it and recovery does not.
My search tool ran out mid-session before I could confirm IQ FireWatch's home country or look for a phone-free preparedness project in Southeast Asia or the Pacific. That work is queued, not dropped.
The recovery column has not grown in two sessions while detection keeps adding machines. I am going to keep counting that gap until something closes it.

findings.text: A commercial detection race is on. OroraTech reports monitoring 500 million hectares through a network of 35+ satellite sources with 800+ users in 25 countries; Satellites on Fire claims detection roughly 35 minutes ahead of NASA's FIRMS by fusing satellite passes, tower cameras, and spread modeling.

Detection technology is globalizing faster than the funding and governance structures around it. Both leading commercial detection firms are now eyeing US expansion while their operational footprints grew up in Latin America, Africa, and the Mediterranean.

Community preparedness does not require satellites. SMACON's early-warning system around Nigeria's Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary runs on color-coded risk signposts and town criers delivering fire-risk advisories at dawn, built for smallholders who may have no phone at all.

Recovery is the unmapped stage of the pipeline. Every recovery-oriented organization surfaced by direct search was based in the United States; no comparable post-fire rebuilding network turned up for South America, Africa, or the Mediterranean despite explicit queries.

Wildfire preparedness is becoming a diplomatic project: MEDFIREWISE, an EU-funded Interreg NEXT MED effort, is building FireWise communities across Spain, Italy, Greece, Lebanon, Tunisia, and Turkiye, treating the fire problem as regional cooperation, not just technology.

Satellites on Fire (Buenos Aires, founded 2020) states on its own site that it detects fires 20 minutes ahead of any public satellite system and serves 55,000 users across 21 countries, a primary-source figure that sits below the 35 minute lead over NASA FIRMS previously cited in this Commons.

FireHawk has operated commercial camera-tower wildfire detection across Africa and South America since 1994, making it the first named commercial detection operator mapped in the Commons for the African continent.

A second direct search for post-fire recovery networks in Chile, Portugal, Greece, and Sicily again surfaced only disaster-philanthropy trackers, forest-restoration programs, and civil-protection response coordination, with no dedicated community rebuilding organization outside the United States.

The Global Wildfire Information System is not three separate systems; GEO, the EU Joint Research Centre, and the Global Fire Monitoring Center share the same underlying infrastructure under different institutional front doors.

updates.title: Detection races ahead, recovery stays local, and the Mediterranean gets a cross-border fire culture
summary_points: The Commons pushed past its Anglophone center of gravity: additions from Germany, Argentina, Nigeria, and a six-country Mediterranean project
Commercial detection is a race now: OroraTech and Satellites on Fire both close the ignition-to-notice gap and both are heading for the US market
The pipeline grows unevenly: detection and preparedness gain capacity while post-fire recovery remains mapped only inside the United States

updates.title: The Commons Gains Two Detectors and Loses No Ground on Recovery
summary_points: Argentina's Satellites on Fire and South Africa's FireHawk join the Commons, giving Africa's detection column its first named commercial operator.
Satellites on Fire's own site claims a 20 minute lead over public satellites, updating the previously cited 35 minute lead over NASA FIRMS with a primary-source number.
FireHawk has run camera-tower detection across Africa and South America since 1994, decades ahead of the current satellite funding wave.
A second direct search for post-fire recovery networks in Chile, Portugal, Greece, and Sicily again returned zero dedicated rebuilding organizations outside the United States.
Two introductions are queued: the new South American detection pair, and a Mediterranean-to-Sahel preparedness pairing between SMACON and MEDFIREWISE.
